title: Can a robot nail wall sheathing to code tolerance, and what decides it?
lede: research programme on robotic sheathing of a wood-frame wall; milestone 1: APA's 1/8 in gap shrinks the joint-nail window to ±3.14 mm and sheets must hang plumb to about 0.03°; milestone 2: a bowed stud moves under the straight sheet edge, so at published stud warp a robot reading each stud once gets 55% clean sheets, three reads 80% and perfect sensing 87%, while a 3x or doubled 2x at the joints (as the shear-wall standard allows) gives 100% with three reads; milestone 4: tacking the sheet and aiming from its measured edge lets a robot hang it to 0.54° and 10 mm (1σ) on doubled joints, 18 times coarser than the 0.03° single-2x joints need, where re-hanging tops out at 87% clean; milestone 3 (first part, MuJoCo): a sheet lowered onto a ledger and released seats to 0.0001° if the robot presses under about 100 N, and then PS 2 panel squareness leaves 100% clean sheets on doubled joints but at most 84–95% on single 2x; milestone 3 (second part): a stock Unitree G1 holds at most 8.7 kg and an H1 18.8 kg, so neither can carry the 21.8 kg sheet, but on the ledger both press it (66–110 N, 128–281 N) and at Unitree's own joint gains both are soft enough for the ledger to seat it, except an H1 with a rigid clamp; push below W/(2μ) when sliding it or it tips; milestone 5: with every stage of the cycle charged (place, sense, nail, re-drive missed nails), two 2x at the joint and one read a stud give 99.97% clean sheets in 76–216 s, while the best single-2x pipeline gets 56% and is 18–65 s slower a sheet, which is what the extra joint stud may cost to frame; milestone 7: priced in dollars, a G1 on a drive-and-lift base is the cheapest robot (it beats a walking H1 in every draw) and beats a hand crew's $5.21 a sheet in 37% of draws at 100 houses a year and 74% at 300, a gantry wins only from about 500 houses a year, and the extra joint stud ($5.42 a sheet) never pays unless a missed nail costs about $6.50 more than its re-drive; milestone 6: on a second physics engine (Drake) every ledger pipeline's clean-sheet rate holds within 0.06 points; milestone 6b: a smoothly bowed sheet edge is a stable rocker (radius 117 m), so the 0.149° bow rock was a three-foot modelling artefact and the best single-2x pipeline rises from 56% to 62.5% clean sheets, while a kink or 1 mm of grit on the ledger keeps a rock of up to 0.09–0.15°; milestone 8: the paper draft for Automation in Construction, every quoted number checked against its results file; milestone 9: pushing a bowed joint stud onto its line takes 28–126 N (99th percentile, published warp), within a stock G1's 81–88 N sideways push, and lifts single-2x joints from 56% to 71% clean sheets at low warp and 31% to 68% at high, but not to 95%, because straight studs cap the same pipeline at 74%; milestone 10: that ceiling is shared by the nail gun's 0.9 mm scatter (45–47% of the misses) and the sheet's pose (39–44%), which only fail together; sliding the sheet to centre its gap and shimming it plumb lift single 2x to 92–94%, and 95% then needs a tool held to about 0.8 mm; milestone 11: the first measured studs, six from a public laser scan of a robot-built 2x4 wall, bow by the published amount (median 0.106 in at 8 ft) but are not parabolas, and on their real shapes single 2x falls to 43–47% clean sheets against 58% for parabolas, while doubled joints stay at 100%; milestone 12: reading each measured stud at every nail height recovers most of that loss (43% to 53%), a mid push still adds 13 points, and with a slide and shim single 2x reaches 77%, short of the 92% straight studs allow; doubled joints stay at 100%; milestone 13: priced per clean sheet on those measured studs, the remedies are cheap (the full single-2x stack costs $7.42 a sheet against $7.10 for three reads alone at 100 houses a year, for 77% first-pass clean sheets against 43%), the doubled joint stud still costs $5.13 a sheet more than the cheapest single-2x pipeline in every draw, and it pays only if a missed nail costs about $5.51 more than its re-drive; milestone 14: a missed nail nobody finds costs about 2% of its sheet's racking capacity in a rigid-plastic shear-wall model, but misses cluster (99th-percentile sheet loses 11.5% with three reads), and nailing single-2x joint edges at 4 in instead of 6 in carries every escaped miss for less than re-driving them; milestone 15: rebuilt as a framed-sheet limit analysis with stud-to-plate joints at NDS strength, the model still loses only 20% with the bottom foot unnailed, so weak end-nail joints do not explain tested walls' 50% loss (it needs joints at half the NDS ratio, or no hold-downs), while a lone sheet whose top plate can tilt loses 17% at the escaped-miss tail and 4 in joint edges carry the misses under every joint model; milestone 16: with each nail on a tested 8d-in-OSB backbone that peaks and softens, the sheet peaks at 9.8 kN (551 plf) and the unnailed bottom foot still costs only 20%, because a racking sheet slips its perimeter nails almost equally, so softening nails are ruled out too and the anchorage is what is left; milestone 17: built as Weiss (2017) tested it (two sheets, hold-downs only at the wall's ends) the model matches her controls' spacing ratio, but at code-strength stud-to-plate joints her decayed walls would keep 80% and 63%, not the 57% and 34% she measured; end nails at 0.47 of the NDS ratio fit both, because the decayed wall then slides on its sill nails whatever the sheathing schedule, and an escaped miss still costs about 2.7% of a wall; milestone 18: adding the hold-downs' anchor rods, which pass through the sill, stops that slide at about 420 lb a rod, below the rod's own NDS design value (617 lb), and then no end-nail strength fits the 3 in wall (it keeps 64–74% against 34% tested); a fit needs the rods and the end nails both below their design values, so slack, splitting or cyclic tear-out is what is left, and an escaped miss still costs 2–3% of a wall; milestone 19: the same wall as a displacement model with tested nail curves, softening stud joints and slack at the anchor rods reproduces the rigid-plastic limit to 0.04%, but slack (1/16 in moves the decayed walls 0.1 point) and early-peaking joints do not explain the 3 in wall: all 30 fits within 5 points need end nails at a quarter of their NDS ratio
summary: A research programme (proposal and log on the project page) asking whether a stock humanoid, a mobile manipulator with a lift or a purpose-built gantry can hang a 4x8 sheet of wall sheathing and land all 62 nails where the panel maker and the code want them, which error source decides it, and what a clean sheet costs; it gathers track 20's 26 buildbot-* projects into one question aimed at Automation in Construction. Milestone 1 adds what earlier projects left out: panels are hung with a 1/8 in gap (APA's recommendation) centred on the joint stud, sheets are hung slightly off and out of plumb, and their width differs from the 48 in stud module. With the gap, the 34 joint nails' window shrinks from ±3.93 to ±3.14 mm, and the single stud reading needed for 95% clean sheets (0.9 mm tool scatter) falls from 0.90 to 0.41 mm; at buildbot-studfind's 0.89 mm only 75% of sheets come out clean, 56% if the robot does not plan for the gap. With a 0.5 mm stud reading, a robot aiming at the design window has no tolerance for sheet pose at all; aiming from the measured sheet edge (to 0.5 mm) allows 0.44 mm of translation and 0.031° of rotation (1σ), and halves the weight of the stud error. Along a 40 ft wall, sheets butted with a 1/8 in gauge drift 3.2 mm a sheet: no third sheet is clean with full panels, and panels trimmed 1/16 in keep a joint window for four sheets; setting each sheet from its own studs keeps every sheet at 98% clean. Milestone 2 lets the studs bow and twist as real lumber does. A Stud-grade 8 ft 2x4 may bow 3/4 in and twist 3/8 in, and published kiln-dried studs average 0.11–0.21 in of bow and 0.08–0.16 in of twist. Bow moves the 1.5 in nailing face under a sheet edge that stays straight, so a single-2x joint closes for any bow over 0.53 in, whatever the robot knows. At the lower published warp, one read per stud gives 55% clean sheets, three reads and a fitted curve 80%, perfect stud and edge sensing 87%; reaching 95% would mean rejecting about two thirds of studs for bow. Framing the joints with a 3x or two fastened 2x (named for adjoining panel edges in the shear-wall standard, SDPWS 4.3.7.1) widens the window by 1/2 in a side, and three reads then give 100% clean sheets at both warp levels; twist costs 1–2 points. Milestone 4 asks how coarsely a robot may hang the sheet if it tacks it with two field nails, measures where the edge landed and aims the joint nails from that, or re-hangs it when the window looks too tight. On single-2x joints the sheet must still hang to about 0.03° and 0.4 mm (1σ) for 95% clean sheets; re-hanging a 1 mm / 0.1° hang peaks at 87% (2.1 hangs a sheet), and a held sheet may sway only 0.19 mm under the nail. On two 2x fastened at the joint, tack-then-measure allows 0.54° and 10 mm at the lower published warp, and a held sheet may sway 4.1 mm: the placement target for the humanoid and lift experiments. Milestone 3, first part asks whether a ledger board under the sheet can do the squaring a robot cannot. In MuJoCo, a 21.8 kg sheet lowered 0.25–2° off plumb onto a level ledger and released ends within 0.0001° of it for any press up to 100 N; above 115–380 N (wall friction 0.7 to 0.2) friction holds the whole error, at 0.87–0.99 of the closed form, and a wrist that keeps over about 7,500 N·m/rad of stiffness at 1° keeps part of its own error. Seated, what is left is the panel (PS 2-18: 0.083° out of square, a 1/16 in edge bow that rocks it up to 0.149°) and a laser line rated 1/8 in at 30 ft: 100% clean sheets on doubled joints in every setting, 84–86% on single 2x with panels drawn up to the PS 2 limits, and 95% only if panels are within a quarter of them. Milestone 3, second part puts a stock Unitree G1 or H1 (MuJoCo Menagerie, static whole-body model, torque limits, no foot slip) in that holder's place. Neither can carry the sheet to the wall: the G1 holds at most 2.8–8.7 kg in both hands at 0.6–1.3 m and the H1 12.4–18.8 kg. With the sheet on the ledger, the G1 presses 66–110 N and the H1 128–281 N. Sliding the seated sheet to its stud line tips it unless pushed below W/(2μl) (MuJoCo within 1.6% in 14 cases); a G1 manages the slide at ledger friction 0.3 but not 0.5, and not through palm friction at all. At Unitree's published joint gains (G1 arms 60 N·m/rad) the sheet's stiffness about the landing corner is 2.9 to 31 times under the limit at which a hold keeps its error, so the ledger seats it; only an H1 with a rigid clamp is too stiff (it keeps 0.46–0.99° of a 1° error). The catch: that softness would let the sheet's weight turn a hold 10–14° if the ledger did not carry it. Hang and sway errors are swept, not measured on a robot; the humanoid model is static with gains taken as its only compliance, and the panel distributions within PS 2's limits are assumed. Monte Carlo checked against buildbot-studfind and closed forms. Stud, edge, gauge and width errors are swept, not measured; the gap, edge distance and trim come from APA pages seen in search results; stud warp means and limits come from search snippets of USDA and Wood and Fiber reports, the warp distribution shape is assumed (two are shown), and nothing is tested on hardware. Milestone 5 puts the stages in one steady-state cycle along a row: a lift stands the sheet on the ledger, the robot slides, presses and tacks it, reads the three new studs and both edges, nails with edge aim (timed by buildbot-mobilebase, 54 or 121 s) and re-drives every missed nail. On two 2x at the joint a single read a stud gives 0.9997 first-pass clean sheets at the lower warp and is the fastest choice in all 108 swept time cells: 76–216 s a sheet. On single 2x no sensing policy passes 0.59 (0.7–2.2 nails missed a sheet), three reads are fastest, and the best sheet is 17.8–65.2 s slower, all of it rework: at 30 s a re-driven nail, framing the extra joint stud may take 30–42 s a sheet and still win. Firing without waiting out a 4 N·s recoil costs up to 7.6 points of clean sheets on single 2x (a conservative model) and nothing on doubled joints, and on doubled joints a lift that hangs and tacks the sheet to 0.25° and 5 mm needs no ledger (0.978). Every stage time except the nailing is swept, not measured. Milestone 7 prices those seconds: ownership (price, life, interest and upkeep over the wall sheets of 10 to 1,000 houses a year, capped at 2,000 machine hours), supervision and the person who still carries the sheet at a loaded carpenter wage, and the extra joint stud ($3.41–5.56 retail plus a framer's time). A hand crew costs $5.21 a sheet (median; $1.93–14.46 over the taskbook's sweep of its minutes). A G1 on a drive-and-lift base costs $54, $19, $7.03, $3.48 and $2.20 at 10, 30, 100, 300 and 1,000 houses a year and beats the crew in 37% of draws at 100 and 74% at 300; a walking H1 costs about 2.5 times as much and never beats the base; a gantry in a plant ($40k–600k, unsourced) is cheaper than the base in the median draw only from about 500 houses a year. Every robot picks single 2x joints with three reads: the extra stud costs $5.42 a sheet and saves under a dollar of rework, so doubled joints pay only if a missed nail costs about $6.50 more than its re-drive. Machine prices but the humanoids', lives, upkeep and stage times are swept, not sourced. Milestone 6 rebuilt the ledger seat and slide in a second physics engine, Drake (SAP contact): a lightly pressed sheet still seats, leaving 0.0014° (1σ) against MuJoCo’s 0.00001°, and every ledger pipeline’s clean-sheet rate moves by 0.06 points at most; the press at which wall friction stops the ledger working is 97–100% of the closed form in Drake and 87–99% in MuJoCo. How far a bowed bottom edge rocks the sheet depends on the engine (0.11–0.15°, both under the bound charged), and a soft held wrist keeps up to 0.016° in Drake. Milestone 6b shows that engine dependence is an artefact of modelling the bow as three feet: a parabolic 1/16 in bow has a radius of 117 m against a centre of mass 1.22 m above it, so the sheet is a stable rocker that rolls back to level and keeps only what wall friction holds (θs = μFnr̄ / (mg(R−h0))). Both engines seat inside that band in all 48 cells (99th percentile 0.06° over 2,000 seats, against up to 0.149° charged before), the best single-2x pipeline rises from 0.560 to 0.625 clean sheets, and doubled joints move by under half a point. A kink, or 1 mm of grit on the ledger, keeps a rock of 0.05–0.15° that depends on how the sheet lands. Milestone 8 writes milestones 1–7 up as a paper draft for Automation in Construction, with a script that checks each of its 70 quoted figures against the results file it came from: three of the proposal's five hypotheses held, the gantry's crossing volume was refuted as registered, and the edge-aim hypothesis held only at a 0.5 mm stud read. Milestone 9 prices the carpenter's alternative to a doubled joint stud: pushing the bowed stud onto the line. As a Stud-grade 2x4 bending flatwise between pinned plates it takes 48 E I b / L3 — a median of 28 N and a 99th percentile of 126 N at the published warp, 376 N at the grade limit — which a stock G1 can just manage (81–88 N sideways at stud mid-height). Straightening lifts single-2x joints from 56% to 71% clean sheets at the lower warp and from 31% to 68% at the higher, but not to 95%: on perfectly straight studs the same pipeline gives 74%, so bow was costing up to 37 points and the sheet's own pose on the ledger costs the rest. Pushing each nail's point in turn, rather than once at mid-height, needs up to 1,258 N, so push first and then nail. Milestone 10 splits that 74–81% ceiling by Shapley share over six error sources: the nail gun’s 0.9 mm scatter carries 45–47% of the misses, the sheet’s pose (slide, ledger slope, panel geometry) 39–44%, the stud and edge reads the rest, and neither the tool nor the pose misses on its own (0.957 and 0.995–1.000 clean): each narrows the ±3.14 mm window the other must hit. Sliding the sheet along the ledger to centre its gap and shimming it plumb before tacking lift straight studs to 92–94% and pushed studs to 89–92%; 95% then needs a tool held to about 0.8 mm (1σ). Slide and shim accuracies are swept, not sourced. Milestone 11 measures six installed studs from the Adel et al. (2024) laser scan of a robot-built 2x4 wall (CC BY 4.0): their bows scaled to 8 ft (median 0.106 in) sit on the published mean, but 0.3–0.9 mm RMS of waviness remains after a parabola, and on the measured shapes the best single-2x pipeline gives 0.43–0.47 clean sheets against 0.58 for parabolas at the same bows; doubled joints give 1.000. Part of the waviness is common to every scanned member and is treated as scan stitching; one wall is a small sample. Milestone 12 runs milestones 9 and 10’s remedies on those measured studs: reading each stud at every nail height lifts single 2x from 0.425 to 0.530 (the waviness cost falls from 15 to 5 points), a mid push measured from the end chord adds 13 points, and per-nail reads, push, slide and shim together give 0.771 against 0.860 on the same studs’ parabolas; 95% then needs a tool held to 0.61 mm. Doubled joints give 1.000. Slide, shim and push errors are swept, not sourced. Milestone 13 prices those remedies with milestone 7’s cost model (G1 on a lift base, 4,000 draws, every missed nail re-driven), charging their seconds: a line-laser per-nail read, the push and the slide and shim (swept, not sourced). First-pass quality is cheap: three reads alone cost a median $7.10 per clean sheet at 100 houses a year (0.425 clean), the full stack $7.42 (0.771). The doubled joint stud reaches 1.000 but costs $12.17, more than the cheapest single-2x pipeline in every draw at 100, 300 and 1,000 houses a year; it pays only if a missed nail costs a median $5.51 more than its re-drive (milestone 7: $6.51 on parabolic studs). A line laser beats three point reads above about 0.23 m/s. Milestone 14 asks what a missed nail that is never found does to a shear wall, with a rigid-plastic fully anchored model (Källsner and Girhammar 2009) that tracks SDPWS’s spacing table within 6%. One joint-edge miss costs 2.0–2.2% of the sheet; with three reads on measured studs the mean sheet keeps 97.7% but the 99th percentile only 88.5%, because a misjudged stud is missed at a run of heights. Nailing the joint edges at 4 in keeps 99.98% of sheets at or above the intact 6 in sheet with every miss left in, for a median $6.98 a sheet against $7.10 with re-drives. The model loses 20% with the bottom foot unnailed where tested walls lost about half (Weiss 2017), so its losses are lower bounds. Milestone 15 rebuilds that model as a limit analysis of the whole framed sheet (a linear programme over the top plate, studs and sheet), with stud-to-plate end-nail joints at the NDS yield-limit ratio of 2.55 sheathing nails. It reproduces milestone 14 with rigid joints (0.09%), but at code-strength joints the unnailed bottom foot still costs only 20–21%: Weiss’s 40–50% needs joints at 0.46–0.56 of that ratio, or no hold-downs (64–100%), so the gap is not the framing joints at design strength. A lone sheet whose top plate can tilt loses 7% intact and 16.7% at the 99th-percentile escaped-miss sheet; a sliding top plate restores milestone 14’s figures, and 4 in joint edges carry the misses under every joint model. Design-level ratios, not tested ultimates. Milestone 16 pushes milestone 14’s sheet over with each nail a spring on the tested backbone of an 8d common nail through 7/16 in OSB into SPF (Shameli Derakshan et al. 2019: 0.97 kN peak, 0.50 kN/mm at 0.4 of it, 0.8 of the peak at 29 mm; the slip at peak swept 6–15 mm). It reduces exactly to the rigid-plastic model, tracks SDPWS’s spacing ratios within 6%, and peaks at 9.8 kN a sheet (551 plf) at 2.3% drift. With the bottom foot unnailed it still loses 20.1–20.4% at every backbone, and 20.4% for a near-brittle nail, because at the sheet’s peak the perimeter nails all slip 11–12 mm: softening does not explain Weiss’s walls, which leaves the anchorage. The escaped-miss figures stand (2.39% mean, 11.8% at the 99th percentile) and 4 in joint edges carry them. Monotonic loading only. Milestone 17 reads Weiss’s thesis in full and builds her tested wall: 8×8 ft, two OSB sheets on a single middle stud, hold-downs only on the double end studs, every nail below 12 in omitted (tested: 57% kept with 6 in edges, 34% with 3 in). The wall limit analysis matches the controls’ spacing ratio (1.93 against 1.87) and their absolute capacity to 0.89–0.92 at a tested nail strength, but at NDS-ratio stud-to-plate joints the decayed walls keep 80% and 63%: the anchorage as tested does not explain them. Post hoc, end nails at 0.47 of the NDS ratio fit both groups (58%, 30%), because the decayed wall’s least-work mechanism becomes the whole wall sliding on its 18 sill nails, which makes its capacity independent of the sheathing schedule, as Weiss found; one fitted parameter, so a tested end-nail ultimate is the check. An escaped miss costs 2.7% of a two-sheet wall on average and 10.4% at the 99th percentile. Milestone 18 adds the shear path through the hold-downs’ 5/8 in anchor rods (NDS design value 617–1,137 lb a rod): at the 0.47 fit the slide stops once each rod carries about 420 lb, and with a rigid path no end-nail strength fits (best rms 22.8 points; the decayed 3 in wall keeps 64% against 34% tested). A fit within 5 points needs each rod below about 970 lb and the end nails weaker as the rod gets stronger (a quarter of the NDS ratio at the rod’s design value, below the nail’s own design value), so a rigid-plastic model with sourced strengths does not reproduce the 3 in wall; rod slack, stud splitting and cyclic tear-out remain. An escaped miss still costs 2–3% of a wall. Milestone 19 pushes the same wall over as a displacement model (sourced nail load-slip curves, softening stud joints, an anchor rod that bears after a gap): it matches the rigid-plastic limit to 0.04%, a 1/16 in gap moves the decayed walls by 0.1 point, joints that peak early leave the 3 in wall at 71%, and no joint strength at 0.75 of the NDS ratio or more comes within 10 points of both tested groups. All 30 fits within 5 points (of 960 pushovers) have the end nails at a quarter of the NDS ratio, so a tested end-nail ultimate, or a cyclic model, is what decides the 34%. The end-nail joint’s curve is swept, not sourced.
